introduction: Historical researches which throw fresh light on the consequences of the Napoleonic invasion of Egypt are a matter of general interest, since the forces set in motion in 1798 are still at work in the life of East and West alike. There are two nations, however, which are concerned in a particularly intimate way: the Egyptians, whose country—with its wonderful productivity and its unrivalled strategic position—has been one of the two focuses of the so-called Eastern Question (the other focus being the Black Sea Straits), and the British, who eventually succeeded to the heritage which Napoleon staked out as a prize to be contended for, through War and Diplomacy, by the Western Powers. The historical work introduced by this foreword has been written, in English, by an Egyptian historian who has made postgraduate studies in two British Universities and is now engaged in public work in his own country. It is to be hoped that an Arabic translation of the book will be published in due course in Egypt, in order that it may be accessible to students of history in both countries. In the opinion of the writer of this prefatory note (who had the pleasure of “supervising” part of Mr. Ghorbal’s researches—a “supervision” in which he learnt more than he taught), Mr. Ghorbal possesses just that combination of qualifications which these researches require. He is in personal touch with both East and West—with the East because it is his home, and with the West because he has lived and studied here—and at the same time he is so thoroughly detached from the passions and prejudices that enter into his field of study that—were not his name printed on the title page—it would be difficult to guess from internal evidence whether the author were an Englishman, a Frenchman, an Egyptian, or none of these. This is a remarkable achievement because these passions and prejudices of more than a century ago are not without a bearing on contemporary controversies between Englishmen and Egyptians. Yet no reflection of contemporary politics can be discerned in Mr. Ghorbal’s work. When it is added that Mr. Ghorbal understands not only the science of extracting information from archives, but the art of presenting the information which he obtains, enough will have been said to show that this book is very well worth reading, if only for the author’s merits. Nor is this one of those good books on bad subjects. The subject which Mr. Ghorbal has chosen to study is as good as can be desired.
passages: Only two days later the French armament appeared off the low-lying coast of Egypt. Leaving Malta on June 19th, it did not take the direct route, but skirted the south coast of Crete. It was off that island that its Commander-in-chief learnt of the presence of seventeen English ships. His anxiety as to the safety of the convoy was greatly increased.

Tracing the attitude of the French Government towards the Army of the East, we find that its first measure was to stop the departure of the second expedition upon whose arrival in Egypt Bonaparte was counting.[492] The cause was the news of the presence of a strong English fleet in the Mediterranean. Nor were the diplomatic measures, as arranged with the same general, carried out.

The foundations of the peace of Europe were laid down in a spirit of rivalry that boded ill for the durability of the structure. The history of the treaties in the making is not less significant than that of the actual struggle which they were to terminate.

“On me croit fou, inconséquent, mais je sais ce qu’il y a à faire mieux que ceux qui me jugent,” once observed the First Consul to Morkoff, the Russian envoy,[1038] and no account of his career can be true which does not credit him with some intelligible motive for his actions.

Drovetti, the vice-consul and head of the establishment after the departure of Lesseps, was in Alexandria all the time. He could not but be struck with the personality of Mehemet Ali.
